posts.cooked:
Okay, so I think I finally figured out a nice easy and logical way to interpret this. Damage count modifiers (unless stated as a response to a trigger, of which I’m not sure there are any) are applied to a global state. Thus far I have concluded there exist a state for each type of damage, each individual player (including villain player and enviromnet player), and a state for all damage (as it’s easier to just create this global state than it is to decide whether all damage means all damage types or all players). Once all other effects have had their turn doing any modification necessary to the damage (including changing the damage type) in order of play, then the damage count modifiers are applied.

This gives a nice consistant flow of logic while adhering Adam’s ruling. (My reason for objection previously is that what I read from the early opposition replies were along the line of “That’s just the way it is” without detailed steps, which never sits well with me. It was a couple of the more recent posts that had enough explaination in it to allow me to come to this conclusion. I still think I like order over everything, but I find this acceptable none the less.)

posts.name: TheJayMann
posts.cooked:
Your example seems rather complicated, and if the rules ended up the way I originally belived, there would be a pipeline to follow. However, first, no card exists (from my memory) that converts damage of one specific type to another, and if there were, it would cause quite a bit of problems, no matter which method were used. One problem being playing a card that converts fire to radiant, then playing a card later that converts fire to cold. In a pipeline mode, the second card would never take effect (except if the first card is cancelled while the second card is still active). In a replacer mode, the second would overcome the first, giving the opposite results. Using a “static” mode, ambiguity would result, with no well defined answer.

But, in the cases listed here, the damage type modifiers follow the same rule of first card played has it’s effects applied first, as to avoid conflict, whereas damage count modifiers (including conditional modifiers) are applied at the summary of damage, as they can’t conflict. Cramped Quarters Combat does a global damage modifire to Melee, and an unconditional damage modifier of +1, Imbued Fire changes all heroes’ damage to fire, and conditionally increases all fire +1. In the case of Cramped Quarters then Imbued Fire, all heroes attack with Fire, all non-heroes attack Melee, all non-heroes gain +1 damage, all heroes gain +1 +1 damage. In the case of Imbued Fire then Cramped Quarters Combat, all characters attack Melee, and all damage is +1.

posts.name: TheJayMann
posts.cooked: You already need to track order of played cards. E.g. the first minion played on the table has his effect before the second minion played. The fact that changing the order of changing damage types can change the effect (they are not commutative) means they have to go by play order. The fact that changing the order damage count modifires do not change the effect (they are commutative) means they don’t have an order, and are determined at the end of battle resolution (a way of saying “they just are” rather than apply them as an effect in a chain).

posts.name: TheJayMann
posts.cooked: The conclusion we came to is the simple ruling that was in the book, just that the explaination was long and drawn out. Basically, the order the cards are played define which one ultimately determines the type (the last card played that changes the damage type gets the say). Then, when the damage is dealt, the damage type is checked for any modifiers which are then applied (if there is a modifier on cold damage, and the damage is ultimately cold, you get the modifier, but if you end up with fire damage, you don’t get the modifier, even if another card “briefly” changed it to cold). Otherwise, you have a crazy time trying to keep up with modifiers (if damage is increased every time a damage type is changed to cold but then not decreased when changed to something else, would cause all sorts of confusion and abuse).

posts.cooked: Well, that one is simple. If The Wraith has Micro Targeting Computer on the table, and she deals projectile damage, then it’s increased by two. If Imbued Fire is played, and she deals projectile damage, it is converted to fire, and then only increased by one, as she actually dealt fire damage, not projectile damage. If something else were to then convert her damage to projectile (say, a Twist the Ether), the increase of one by Imbued Fire would no longer apply, but the increase of two from Micro Targeting Computer would (reset to increase by two, not increase by three).
